subject: chemistry
overview: This unit introduces the p-block elements of Groups 13 to 18. Their valence electrons enter p-orbitals, so the block contains metals, metalloids, non-metals and noble gases. NEET mainly tests electronic configurations, periodic trends with their exceptions, the inert pair effect, oxidation states and the anomalous behaviour of the first member of each group. These questions are usually short statement-based or order-based MCQs.

topics.explanation: The p-block has six groups. Group 13 is the boron family: B, Al, Ga, In, Tl and Nh. Group 14 is the carbon family: C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb and Fl. Group 15 is the nitrogen family (pnictogens): N, P, As, Sb, Bi and Mc. Group 16 is the oxygen family (chalcogens): O, S, Se, Te, Po and Lv. Group 17 is the halogens: F, Cl, Br, I, At and Ts. Group 18 is the noble gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn and Og. The block shows the full range of character. Non-metals cluster at the upper right, metalloids lie along the diagonal (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) and metals sit at the lower left (Al, Ga, In, Tl, Sn, Pb, Bi, Po). Metallic character increases down each group and decreases across a period. He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe and Rn are monatomic gases.
key_points: p-block spans Groups 13 to 18, which is six groups.
Common names are boron family, carbon family, pnictogens, chalcogens, halogens and noble gases.
Metalloids are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te.
B is non-metallic (often classed as a metalloid) while Al, Ga, In and Tl are metals.
In Group 14, C is a non-metal, Si and Ge are metalloids, and Sn and Pb are metals.
In Group 15, N and P are non-metals, As and Sb are metalloids, and Bi is a metal.
Po is a radioactive metal and At is a radioactive halogen.
He is placed in Group 18 although it has no p-electrons.

formulas.meaning: Relates p-block group number to valence electrons (ns plus np).

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks you to identify metalloids or classify elements as metal or non-metal, often hidden inside statement questions.

topics.explanation: The general valence configuration of the p-block is $ns^2np^{1-6}$, with He as the exception at $1s^2$. Valence configurations by group are: Group 13 $ns^2np^1$, Group 14 $ns^2np^2$, Group 15 $ns^2np^3$, Group 16 $ns^2np^4$, Group 17 $ns^2np^5$ and Group 18 $ns^2np^6$. The core differs down a group. Second and third period elements have a noble gas core only. From period 4 onwards a filled $(n-1)d^{10}$ subshell appears, as in Ga, Ge and As. From period 6 onwards a filled $4f^{14}$ subshell is also present, as in Tl, Pb and Bi. These poorly shielding d and f electrons raise the effective nuclear charge. That causes anomalies such as Ga being smaller than Al and the inert pair effect. Examples are Al $[Ne]3s^23p^1$, Ga $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^24p^1$ and Tl $[Xe]4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^26p^1$.
key_points: General valence configuration is $ns^2np^{1-6}$; He is $1s^2$.
Number of valence electrons equals group number minus 10.
Ga, Ge, As, Se, Br and Kr contain a filled $3d^{10}$ core.
Tl, Pb, Bi, Po, At and Rn contain filled $4f^{14}5d^{10}$ cores.
N has a half-filled $2p^3$ configuration, which gives it extra stability.
Noble gases have a completely filled $ns^2np^6$ shell, which explains their high IE and inertness.

formulas.meaning: Number of p-electrons in the valence shell.
Highest oxidation state shown by the group, e.g. +3 for Group 13 and +5 for Group 15.

topics.neet_tip: Expect questions linking configuration to anomalies, such as the $3d^{10}$ core explaining why Ga is smaller than Al, or the $4f^{14}$ core explaining the inert pair effect in Tl and Pb.

topics.explanation: Across a period atomic radius decreases, while ionisation enthalpy (IE) and electronegativity increase. Non-metallic character and acidic nature of oxides also increase. Down a group atomic radius and metallic character increase, while IE and electronegativity generally decrease. Several irregularities are important. Ga (135 pm) is smaller than Al (143 pm). The Group 13 IE order is B > Tl > Ga > Al > In. In Group 14, Pb has a higher IE than Sn. Group 13 electronegativity falls from B to Al and then rises slightly. Cl has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, and S has a more negative value than O. The inert pair effect makes the lower oxidation state more stable down the group. Thus $Tl^+$, $Pb^{2+}$ and $Bi^{3+}$ are favoured, and $Pb^{4+}$ and $Bi^{5+}$ act as oxidants. Oxides become more basic down a group: $B_2O_3$ is acidic, $Al_2O_3$ is amphoteric and $Tl_2O$ is basic. For hydrides, thermal stability falls down the group while acidic strength or reducing power rises.
key_points: Group 13 atomic radius order is B < Ga < Al < In < Tl.
Group 13 first IE order is B > Tl > Ga > Al > In.
Group 14 first IE order is C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn.
Inert pair effect: stability of the (group OS − 2) state increases down Groups 13 to 15.
Down Group 13, the +1 state becomes more stable relative to +3; $Tl^+$ is more stable than $Tl^{3+}$.
Group 15 hydrides: basicity and thermal stability follow $NH_3 > PH_3 > AsH_3 > SbH_3 > BiH_3$, while reducing power increases down the group.
Group 15 hydride boiling points: $PH_3 < AsH_3 < NH_3 < SbH_3 < BiH_3$.
Acid strength of Group 16 hydrides is $H_2O < H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te$, and of hydrogen halides is $HF < HCl < HBr < HI$.
Halogen bond dissociation enthalpy order is $Cl_2 > Br_2 > F_2 > I_2$.
Electron gain enthalpy: Cl is more negative than F, and S is more negative than O.
Noble gases have the highest IE in each period and positive electron gain enthalpy.
Ga has a very low melting point (about 303 K) but a high boiling point, so it is liquid over a wide range.

formulas.meaning: Oxidation state stabilised by the inert pair effect, e.g. Tl(+1), Pb(+2), Bi(+3).
Common negative oxidation state of non-metals, e.g. N(−3), O(−2), F(−1).

topics.neet_tip: Order-based MCQs dominate this topic, especially IE of Group 13, atomic radius of Al vs Ga, hydride properties and inert pair stability.
topics.topic: General trends in physical and chemical properties across periods and down groups

topics.explanation: The first member of each of Groups 13 to 17 (B, C, N, O, F) differs from its heavier congeners for four reasons: small size, high electronegativity, high ionisation enthalpy and absence of d-orbitals. The first member of Group 18 is He. A second-period element has only four valence orbitals (2s and three 2p). Its maximum covalency is therefore 4, so B forms $[BF_4]^-$ but not $[BF_6]^{3-}$. Al, by contrast, forms $[AlF_6]^{3-}$ because it has vacant 3d orbitals. Small size allows strong $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonding, as in $C=C$, $C\equiv C$, $N\equiv N$ and $O=O$. Heavier members prefer single bonds or $d\pi-p\pi$ bonding. Further examples follow. C shows the strongest catenation. N exists as a diatomic gas, and no $NCl_5$ exists, while $PCl_5$ does. O shows −2 in most compounds and +2 only in $OF_2$. F shows only −1 and has an unusually weak F–F bond due to lone pair repulsion. $NH_3$, $H_2O$ and $HF$ have abnormally high boiling points due to hydrogen bonding.
key_points: The causes of anomalous behaviour are small size, high EN, high IE and no d-orbitals.
Second-period elements have 4 valence orbitals, so their maximum covalency is 4.
Al and heavier elements can expand covalency up to 6 using d-orbitals.
The first members form $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds; heavier members mostly do not.
N cannot form $NCl_5$ or $NF_5$, whereas P forms $PCl_5$.
N2 is a gas, while P exists as $P_4$; O2 is a gas, while S exists as $S_8$.
F shows only −1, has a low F–F bond enthalpy and a less negative electron gain enthalpy than Cl.
H-bonding gives high boiling points to $NH_3$, $H_2O$ and $HF$.
C shows the maximum catenation; Si shows much less because the Si–Si bond is weaker.
Boron halides are monomeric electron-deficient Lewis acids, whereas $AlCl_3$ dimerises to $Al_2Cl_6$.

formulas.meaning: Explains why B, C, N and O cannot exceed covalency 4.

topics.neet_tip: NEET frames statement questions on maximum covalency, number of valence orbitals, $p\pi-p\pi$ bonding and the non-existence of compounds like $NCl_5$ or $[BF_6]^{3-}$.
topics.topic: Unique behaviour of the first element in each group

formula_sheet.meaning: General valence configuration of the p-block (He is $1s^2$).
Valence electron count for Groups 13 to 18.
Common negative oxidation state of non-metals.
Stabilised lower oxidation state down the group: $Tl^+$, $Pb^{2+}$, $Bi^{3+}$.
Atomic radius order in Group 13; Ga is smaller than Al because of poor d-shielding.
First ionisation enthalpy order in Group 13.
First ionisation enthalpy order in Group 14.
Order of basicity and thermal stability of Group 15 hydrides.
Boiling point order of Group 15 hydrides; $NH_3$ is anomalous due to H-bonding.
Bond dissociation enthalpy of halogens; F–F is weak due to lone pair repulsion.
Order of negative electron gain enthalpy of halogens.
Basic character of oxides increases down a group.
Maximum covalency is 4 for B and 6 for Al.
N has no d-orbitals to expand its octet.
Aluminium chloride dimerises to complete its octet; $BCl_3$ stays monomeric.
The only common positive oxidation state of oxygen, since F is more electronegative.

common_traps: Assuming atomic radius always increases down Group 13: Ga (135 pm) is actually smaller than Al (143 pm) because the $3d^{10}$ electrons shield poorly.
Writing the Group 13 IE order as steadily decreasing: the correct order is B > Tl > Ga > Al > In, because of poor shielding by d and f electrons.
Thinking F has the most negative electron gain enthalpy: Cl has, because the small 2p shell of F suffers strong electron–electron repulsion.
Assuming F2 has the strongest halogen bond: the order is $Cl_2 > Br_2 > F_2 > I_2$.
Believing B can show covalency 6 like Al: B has only four valence orbitals (2s, 2p), so its maximum covalency is 4.
Treating $Tl^{3+}$ and $Pb^{4+}$ as stable: inert pair effect makes $Tl^+$ and $Pb^{2+}$ more stable, so $Tl^{3+}$ and $Pb^{4+}$ are oxidising agents.

Expecting $NH_3$ to have the highest boiling point among Group 15 hydrides: $SbH_3$ and $BiH_3$ boil higher because of greater van der Waals forces, though $NH_3$ is still higher than $PH_3$ and $AsH_3$.
Calling oxygen strictly −2 always: it shows −1 in peroxides and +2 in $OF_2$, while F shows only −1.
quick_revision: The p-block spans Groups 13 to 18 with valence configuration $ns^2np^{1-6}$; He is $1s^2$.
Metalloids are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te; metallic character rises down a group.
Ga is smaller than Al, and Group 13 IE order is B > Tl > Ga > Al > In.
The inert pair effect makes $Tl^+$, $Pb^{2+}$ and $Bi^{3+}$ more stable than higher states.
Oxides turn from acidic to amphoteric to basic down a group, e.g. $B_2O_3$, $Al_2O_3$, $Tl_2O_3$.
Group 15 hydride basicity and stability decrease from $NH_3$ to $BiH_3$, while reducing power increases.
Hydride acidity increases down Groups 16 and 17, so HI is the strongest and HF the weakest hydrogen halide.
Cl has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, and the bond enthalpy order is $Cl_2 > Br_2 > F_2 > I_2$.
Period 2 elements have maximum covalency 4, so B forms $[BF_4]^-$ only, while Al forms $[AlF_6]^{3-}$.
First members form $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds ($N\equiv N$, $O=O$, $C=C$); C shows maximum catenation.
$NCl_5$ does not exist but $PCl_5$ does; F shows only −1, and O shows +2 only in $OF_2$.
H-bonding raises the boiling points of $NH_3$, $H_2O$ and $HF$ above those of their next congeners.
